name: Aisha Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Aisha Baker, 58, and I drive a shuttle car underground at a large mine. I check the cable and brakes, then move cut material from the face to the belt while keeping clear of people on foot. I like the teamwork when everyone calls their position, but a shift with a damaged cable is exhausting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your household look like now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rose works full time at a clinic, and our children are grown and live away. We have around ten months of expenses saved because my mine pay is above the usual rate for this job. I have a vocational certificate, and there are several other mines within reach, though I would rather avoid another long commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a quicker shift report is fine, provided someone still checks the cable before we move. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy a note, but I read the result. No software has ever smelled hot insulation from my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect the same work and a solid wage. Rose’s clinic job and our ten-month cushion make this a fairly comfortable picture. We would keep saving rather than spend as if retirement were already paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep driving the shuttle car and making the brake and cable check each shift. I’d add one hundred to our monthly savings transfer while my current wage continues. In the first year after the form changes, I’d compare the digital handover against my own notebook for missing faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm and a little relieved. The paperwork may become shorter, and the part of the job that keeps people safe remains visible. I could discuss retirement with Rose without a deadline hanging over us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a missing fault look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A frayed cable sleeve can be written down as a minor mark even when it needs the fitter. I’d point to the place on the cable and ask for a repair before taking the car back in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does one hundred extra mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is a manageable addition to the savings transfer while both our pay packets arrive. Our children pay their own housing costs now, so we can put that amount toward later years.

I’d still read any **AI note** before handing it to the next shift.
think: My **mine wage** and Rose’s clinic income look secure.
Our **ten-month cushion** gives us room to keep building retirement savings.
do: Drive the **shuttle car** after brake and cable checks.
Add **one hundred monthly** to our savings transfer while wages continue.
Compare digital handovers with my **fault notebook**.
feel: **Calm** about continued work and a shorter report.
S0.quote: No software has ever smelled hot insulation from my seat.
fieldNote: Aisha sometimes uses **AI for notes**, yet physical cable faults and an accurate handover remain her main safety concerns.
Two incomes and a **ten-month cushion** let her increase savings rather than spend the surplus now.

steps.text: Keep driving the shuttle car after brake and cable checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that booking and purchasing can move onto screens long before a robot drives my shuttle car. I would ask the safety committee to check any new traffic plan with operators present. A timetable written upstairs cannot see someone walking beside a stalled belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own paid shifts would continue for now, and other mines nearby could use an experienced driver. But Rose’s clinic does a lot of booking and records work, so her hours might be cut before mine. I would watch that risk even with ten months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask Rose what booking tasks her clinic is already moving to software, then compare our bills with one lower income. I’d attend the mine safety committee’s next traffic-plan review and keep driving my assigned shifts. In the first year I’d try the approved route display beside the existing markers and report any conflict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about Rose’s work and curious about whether the display helps underground. I would not announce a family emergency on the strength of a new screen. We have enough saved to make a careful decision if her hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if Rose lost hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would pause the long trip we planned for next spring before touching housing or medicine. I would not cut it today without an actual change to her roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What conflict might the route display miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A parked maintenance trolley can force walkers into a lane that looked clear when the map was made. I would stop the car and tell the shift lead, then mark the spot for the next crew.

I’d ask for **operator review** of new underground traffic plans.
think: My **driving shifts** should continue, with other local mines as options.
Rose’s **clinic hours** could shrink as booking and records move to software.

Try the approved **route display** against underground markers.
feel: **Uneasy** about Rose’s hours, while able to check the facts.
S1.quote: A timetable written upstairs cannot see someone walking beside a stalled belt.
fieldNote: Aisha locates the near-term income risk in **Rose’s clinic work**, which includes booking and records, before mine robots arrive.
Her **traffic review** is specific to pedestrians and stalled equipment; she will test the screen against physical markers.

steps.text: Keep driving assigned shuttle-car shifts after cable checks
Try the approved route display against underground markers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 could change Rose’s clinic work immediately, while hands-on shuttle-car robots follow around 2031. I would ask both employers for written plans and ask our safety committee who signs off a robot route. We need dates before slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the clinic work is exposed and 63 when robots can drive as well as I can. If my partner Rose loses clinic hours first and then I lose mine wages, even ten months of expenses will not cover years to retirement. Several nearby mines may buy the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d sit with Rose this week and price our household bills on her reduced hours and my full wage. I’d request my retirement statement and apply for a posted driver opening at a nearby mine if this one announces a firm cut. In 2029 I’d continue paid shuttle-car shifts if available, and we would pause the planned trip once either roster actually shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious because the two wages could be hit in sequence. We have a cushion and choices, so I can still do the arithmetic and apply elsewhere. I would be angry if either employer gave us dates only after shifts were removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another mine protect the wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe only for a while. I would read the posted contract and ask whether that mine has already ordered robot vehicles. A local vacancy is useful, but I would not call it safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety committee need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named person who can stop a robot route when a pedestrian enters the lane. I would bring that requirement to the committee meeting before the mine tests one underground.

say: I’d ask both employers for written **workforce plans**.
I’d demand a named **robot-route safety officer** before underground trials.
think: Rose could lose **clinic hours** in 2028, then I could lose driving wages around 2031.
Our **ten-month cushion** would not fund several years without mine pay.
do: Price household **bills** against lower clinic hours this week.
Apply for a posted **local driver job** after a firm mine cut.
Continue paid shifts in **2029** and pause travel after either roster shrinks.
feel: **Anxious** about sequential income losses, with savings and local vacancies giving options.
S2.quote: If my partner Rose loses clinic hours first and then I lose mine wages, even ten months of expenses will not cover years to retirement.
fieldNote: Aisha’s risk is **sequential income loss**: clinic desk work in 2028 and capable shuttle-car robots around 2031.
She will continue paid **2029 driving shifts** and pursue a real local vacancy if her mine confirms cuts.

steps.text: Keep driving paid shuttle-car shifts in 2029 if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that full thinking AI in 2031 gives the clinic and mine more warning, but shuttle-car robots around 2034 still need a safe route. I would ask our union branch to put notice and retraining terms on the next meeting agenda. A warning only helps if someone uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when Rose’s desk tasks face full AI and 66 when robots reach my driving work. That may be close to retirement, but I have not confirmed the amount we would receive. If Rose’s hours fall, our comfortable cushion might become a shorter bridge than it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get both our retirement statements this year and put the clinic and mine pay into separate columns. I’d keep my driving shifts and attend the union branch meeting to vote on notice terms. In 2032 I’d compare the actual clinic roster with our plan before accepting any mine exit offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, but a five-year calendar is something we can use. I would want Rose in the room for the numbers. We could not call a reduced clinic roster harmless just because my wage is still high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What notice term would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a clear minimum notice period before any driver reduction and paid access to actual vacancies. I’d vote for those terms at the branch meeting, though no agreement can promise a job forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a mine exit offer at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our combined retirement income and Rose’s real roster covered the bills. I would not trade a higher mine wage for a lump sum based on a guess.

say: I’d say the **five-year warning** needs a union agenda and real safety plans.
I’d ask for written **notice terms** before driver cuts.
think: At **66** when robots arrive, retirement might work but remains unverified.
Rose’s future **clinic roster** affects how long our cushion lasts.
do: Get both **retirement statements** and separate our income columns.
Keep paid shifts and vote at the **union meeting**.
Compare the **2032 clinic roster** with any mine exit offer.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to plan with a longer calendar and actual figures.
S3.quote: A warning only helps if someone uses it.
fieldNote: Aisha treats the **2034 robot date** as potentially near retirement, while Rose’s clinic hours remain a key household variable.
She plans a **union vote** on notice and vacancies, without assuming the agreement guarantees a future post.

steps.text: Keep driving paid shuttle-car shifts while available
Attend the union branch meeting and vote on driver notice terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade should be enough to record our safe traffic rules and put younger drivers beside experienced ones. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I’d be 68, and shuttle-car robots around 2039, when I’d be 71. I hope to leave the driver’s seat before that machine turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect to drive at 71, though I cannot promise we can retire at 68 without the figures. Rose might still want clinic work even if software changes her role. Our savings and several nearby mines give us room to choose over the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d review our retirement accounts with Rose every January and keep adding to the savings pot while I earn. I’d continue paid shuttle-car shifts while health and mine work allow, and write up the pedestrian checks for our next driver. In 2037 I’d leave the mine only if our combined income covered the regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own working life with robots still so far away. I’d still care about what the mine teaches the next crew. Ten years could let us retire deliberately instead of running from a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which checks would you write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d describe the blind bend near the belt transfer and when to stop for people on foot. I would walk it with the next driver if the mine gave us a shared shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the accounts fall short in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep a paid driving shift if offered or apply at one of the nearby mines while I am able. Rose and I would revise the date, not pretend the bills had gone away.

say: I’d use the **decade** to pass on underground traffic checks.
I hope to leave the **shuttle car** before robots arrive around 2039.
think: At **68** in 2036, retirement depends on our combined income.
Our **savings and local jobs** give us choices while we decide.
do: Review **retirement accounts** with Rose each January.
Keep paid shuttle-car shifts and document **pedestrian checks**.
Test **2037 income** against bills before leaving mine work.
feel: **Calm** about my own work, with concern for future driver training.
S4.quote: Ten years could let us retire deliberately instead of running from a machine.
fieldNote: Aisha expects the **2039 robot date** after her preferred driving years, with a decision based on both partners’ actual income.
She wants the next driver to learn the **blind bend** and pedestrian stops through notes and a shared shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because Rose could lose clinic hours before robots reach my shuttle car at 63. Written plans from both employers, protected pedestrian checks and real local vacancies would help. Savings buy us time, but the two wages pay the running bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to a person walking underground when a robot’s route looks clear on paper. A stopped belt changes where people step. I want someone at the mine named and able to stop the machine.

headlineQuote: Savings buy us time, but the two wages pay the running bills.
portrait: Aisha, **58**, drives a shuttle car underground and checks its cable, brakes and pedestrian routes.
Her **higher mine pay** and Rose’s clinic income support a ten-month savings cushion.
She tries **AI tools occasionally** and wants operators involved in safety reviews.
Fast AGI could hit **clinic hours** before robots threaten her paid driving work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Aisha most because Rose’s hours may fall before shuttle-car robots reach her at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Written **employer plans**, pedestrian safeguards and genuine local vacancies would help the household respond.
